blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a 2015 survey paper by Serban et al. that catalogs datasets and techniques for building data-driven dialogue systems (chatbots). While the paper includes a comprehensive list of dialogue corpora across domains, it also provides a high-level survey of machine learning methods used in dialogue systems, focusing on corpus-based learning. Colyer highlights the distinction between goal-driven systems (e.g., travel assistants) and non-goal-driven systems (e.g., language learning tools), noting that most commercial chatbots fall into the former category. He emphasizes the importance of discriminative models and supervised learning in dialogue systems, as well as the challenges of generating natural responses, especially in multi-turn conversations. The blog post also discusses the differences between spoken and written dialogues, the role of external knowledge in chatbots, and the need for long-term interaction corpora to handle ambiguity and grounding in conversations.
paper_title: A survey of available corpora for building data-driven dialogue systems
paper_abstract: During the past decade, several areas of speech and language understanding have witnessed substantial breakthroughs from the use of data-driven models. In the area of dialogue systems, the trend is less obvious, and most practical systems are still built through significant engineering and expert knowledge. Nevertheless, several recent results suggest that data-driven approaches are feasible and quite promising. To facilitate research in this area, we have carried out a wide survey of publicly available datasets suitable for data-driven learning of dialogue systems. We discuss important characteristics of these datasets, how they can be used to learn diverse dialogue strategies, and their other potential uses. We also examine methods for transfer learning between datasets and the use of external knowledge. Finally, we discuss appropriate choice of evaluation metrics for the learning objective.

figures.title: Standard architecture for dialogue systems
figures.caption: The standard architecture for dialogue systems, shown in Figure 1, incorporates a Speech Recognizer, Language Interpreter, State Tracker, Response Generator, Natural Language Generator, and Speech Synthesizer.
